title: Individual variation in the calls of common marmosets: a marker of social bond strength?
abstract: We recorded contact calls (phee calls) from 24 adult common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) housed in established pair bonds and in newly formed pairs. Using acoustic feature extraction and linear discriminant analysis, we found that marmosets in long-established bonds showed significantly greater acoustic convergence in their phee calls compared to recently paired individuals. Playback experiments demonstrated that animals responded more strongly to recordings of their partner's calls than to those of unfamiliar individuals. These results suggest that phee call structure may encode information about social bond strength and familiarity, and that acoustic convergence may be a marker of pair-bond quality in this cooperatively breeding primate.

title: Neural correlates of vocal learning in juvenile songbirds: a comparative fMRI study
abstract: We used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to compare neural activation patterns during song playback in juvenile and adult zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata) and Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata domestica). Juvenile birds in the sensitive period for vocal learning showed significantly greater activation in the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP), particularly the lateral magnocellular nucleus of the anterior nidopallium (LMAN), compared to adults with crystallised songs. Activation in HVC and RA did not differ significantly by age. These findings support a role for the AFP in evaluating auditory feedback during vocal learning and suggest that neural plasticity in this circuit is developmentally regulated.

title: Temporal structure of dawn chorus in tropical forest birds: acoustic partitioning across species
abstract: We conducted 90 days of passive acoustic monitoring in a lowland tropical forest in Borneo to characterise the timing and acoustic properties of dawn chorus vocalisations across 47 bird species. Species-specific onset times of morning singing were significantly non-random and correlated with bill morphology, body mass, and habitat stratum use. Acoustic niche modelling revealed that species with overlapping frequency ranges tended to sing at different times, consistent with acoustic partitioning. Recording data are available at the Macaulay Library (ML_Borneo_DawnChorus_2021).
